subject: Architecture
title: Chinese Dougong: Brackets That Flex
description: A short lesson to help you apply Chinese Dougong: Brackets That Flex.

hook.text: Chinese buildings have survived earthquakes for 1,000 years using no nails — just interlocking wood brackets.

buildup.text: Dougong brackets stack wooden blocks and arms to transfer roof weight outward and down through columns.

discovery.text: The Yingxian Wooden Pagoda, built in 1056 AD, has survived seven major earthquakes — all without nails.

twist.text: Dougong brackets flex slightly during quakes, absorbing energy that would crack rigid stone buildings.

climax.text: Forbidden City buildings use 230,000 dougong brackets. Each one carved and fitted by master joiners.

punchline.text: No nails, no glue, no bolts. A thousand years of standing on joinery alone.

quiz.question: How do dougong brackets help buildings survive earthquakes?
options: They anchor the building deep into bedrock
They flex slightly, absorbing seismic energy
They detach from the roof, letting it collapse safely

details.summary: Dougong are interlocking wooden bracket systems used in Chinese architecture for over 2,000 years. These clusters of blocks and arms transfer roof weight to columns without nails.
details.whyItMatters: Dougong demonstrate that flexible connections outperform rigid ones in earthquake zones. This principle, understood in China for millennia, is now validated by modern structural engineering and incorporated into contemporary seismic design.
takeaways: Dougong are interlocking brackets transferring roof loads to columns
No nails needed — blocks interlock through precise carpentry
Flexible joints absorb earthquake energy for seismic resistance

faq.question: How do dougong resist earthquakes?
faq.answer: The interlocking pieces can shift slightly under stress and return to position, like a shock absorber. This flexibility dissipates seismic energy that would crack rigid masonry. The Yingxian Pagoda, built in 1056, has survived multiple major earthquakes using this system.

faq.question: Are dougong still used in modern buildings?
faq.answer: Traditional dougong craftsmanship is rare in new construction but is maintained for restoration work on historic buildings. Modern architects sometimes reference dougong aesthetically, and the engineering principle of flexible connections now informs earthquake-resistant steel frame design.
